source_batch.unit_label: Module B unit 8: Basel III Framework on Liquidity Standards

facts.statement: The global financial crisis showed that Basel II left banks wide discretion in computing risk weights and that banks relied heavily on wholesale funding. The courseware lists four ways Basel III responded: higher and better capital with buffers (for India, the courseware says the minimum capital adequacy ratio moved from 9 per cent to 11.5 per cent with a first trigger at 11.5 per cent and a second at 9 per cent, the latter bringing Prompt Corrective Action); limits on the discretion of banks to use complex internal models, with floors on risk weights; a non-risk-based leverage ratio as a backstop; and two liquidity standards, the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR). The Basel Committee issued the international liquidity framework in December 2010. The two standards are complementary: the LCR promotes short-term resilience by ensuring enough high quality liquid assets (HQLA) to survive an acute stress lasting 30 days, and the NSFR promotes resilience over a longer horizon of one year by requiring more stable funding sources. Five monitoring tools supplement them.

The LCR is the stock of high quality liquid assets divided by total net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar days, and a bank must maintain it at a minimum of 100 per cent on an ongoing basis, striving for a higher ratio; the stock is intended to be a defence against the onset of stress, so during financial stress a bank may use HQLA and let the ratio fall below 100 per cent, but must immediately report the shortfall to the Department of Supervision of the Reserve Bank, with reasons and corrective steps. The objective is for the stock to enable survival until day 30, by which time corrective action is assumed. Under the Directions the framework applies to an Indian bank on a standalone and a consolidated basis, and to a foreign bank's branches in India on a standalone basis (the courseware describes the earlier position, standalone for Indian banks with consolidation as an aim). The courseware recounts the phase-in (60 per cent in 2015 rising by ten points a year to 100 per cent in 2019) and the pandemic relaxation (80 per cent from 17 April 2020, 90 per cent from 1 October 2020, 100 per cent again from 1 April 2021). The stress scenario combines a bank-specific and market-wide shock: run-off of a proportion of retail deposits, partial loss of unsecured wholesale funding, partial loss of secured short-term financing, additional outflows from a credit rating downgrade of up to three notches including collateral posting, higher collateral haircuts or collateral needs from market volatility, unscheduled draws on committed credit and liquidity facilities, and the need to buy back debt or honour non-contractual obligations to mitigate reputational risk.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 499-501, sections 18.1.1, 18.1.2 and 18.2; Directions paragraphs 100 to 105

facts.statement: High quality liquid assets are unencumbered assets that can be readily sold or used as collateral to obtain funds in stress with little or no loss of value; the fundamental characteristics are low credit and market risk, ease and certainty of valuation, low correlation with risky assets and listing on a developed, recognised exchange, and the market-related characteristics are an active and sizeable market, committed market makers, low market concentration and flight to quality. Level 1 assets are included without limit and without haircut (cash including reserves in excess of the required CRR, overnight balances under the Standing Deposit Facility, Government securities in excess of the minimum SLR, marketable zero-risk-weight foreign sovereign securities that meet conditions); Directions provide that from 1 April 2026 Level 1 Government securities attract the haircuts of the Liquidity Adjustment Facility and Marginal Standing Facility. Within the mandatory SLR, Government securities count to the extent allowed under the Marginal Standing Facility (currently 2 per cent of net demand and time liabilities, NDTL) and the Facility to Avail Liquidity for Liquidity Coverage Ratio (FALLCR), currently 16 per cent of NDTL in the Directions (the courseware says 9 per cent). FALLCR is available only in stress after all other HQLA are used and on a declaration to that effect, for a tenor of up to 90 days, with the MSF haircuts and a rate 200 basis points above the LAF repo rate. Level 2 assets, after haircuts, are at most 40 per cent of the stock; Level 2A carries a minimum 15 per cent haircut and Level 2B a minimum 50 per cent haircut and at most 15 per cent of the stock. The stock is Level 1 + Level 2A + Level 2B less the adjustment for the 15 per cent cap less the adjustment for the 40 per cent cap, where the 15 per cent cap adjustment is the larger of (adjusted Level 2B − 15/85 × (adjusted Level 1 + adjusted Level 2A)), (adjusted Level 2B − 15/60 × adjusted Level 1) and zero, and the 40 per cent cap adjustment is the larger of ((adjusted Level 2A + adjusted Level 2B − the 15 per cent adjustment) − 2/3 × adjusted Level 1) and zero.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 501-502, sections 18.2.1; Directions paragraphs 114 to 116, 139 to 144, 148 and 149

facts.statement: Total net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar days equal total expected cash outflows less the smaller of total expected cash inflows and 75 per cent of total expected cash outflows. Outflows are outstanding balances multiplied by run-off or draw-down rates; inflows are contractual receivables multiplied by inflow rates and capped in aggregate at 75 per cent of outflows. A bank must not double count: an asset in the HQLA stock cannot also produce an inflow. Retail deposits are demand and term deposits of natural persons (including foreign currency deposits). Stable deposits are those insured by the DICGC to the extent covered, in transactional or relationship accounts; others are less stable. The run-off rates in the liquidity return are 5 per cent for stable and 10 per cent for less stable retail deposits; from 1 April 2026 retail deposits enabled with internet and mobile banking carry an additional 2.5 per cent (7.5 per cent stable and 12.5 per cent less stable), and the same applies to unsecured wholesale funding from non-financial small business customers that is so enabled. Small business customer funding is treated like retail only if the aggregated funding from the customer is up to ₹7.5 crore. Unsecured wholesale funding is funding from non-natural persons not collateralised by specific assets and callable or maturing within 30 days or of undetermined maturity.
facts.locator: Directions paragraphs 156 to 168 and Annex II (BLR-1); the courseware pages read do not give run-off rates

facts.statement: Beyond the two standards the framework prescribes five monitoring tools: contractual maturity mismatch (the gaps between contractual inflows and outflows by time band, showing reliance on maturity transformation, captured through the structural liquidity statement), concentration of funding (funding from each significant counterparty, product or instrument and currency, to encourage diversification), available unencumbered assets (quantity and characteristics of assets that could be collateral), LCR by significant currency (since the standard is met in one currency but currency mismatches matter) and market-related monitoring tools (high frequency market data as early warning). The Basel III liquidity returns are BLR-1 (LCR, monthly), BLR-2 (funding concentration, monthly), BLR-3 (available unencumbered assets, quarterly), BLR-4 (LCR by significant currency, monthly) and BLR-5 (other information on liquidity, monthly); banks must be able to raise the LCR reporting to weekly or daily in stress if directed. LCR disclosure follows the Reserve Bank's disclosure Directions; the courseware says the disclosure in annual financial statements should cover all four quarters of the year. The courseware's time limits for submitting these returns are not in the Directions.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 503-504, sections 18.3 and 18.3.2; Directions paragraphs 195 to 204, 284

facts.statement: The Net Stable Funding Ratio is available stable funding (ASF) divided by required stable funding (RSF), with a minimum of 100 per cent maintained on an ongoing basis and reported quarterly; it covers a one-year horizon, limits overreliance on short-term wholesale funding and encourages better assessment of funding risk across on and off-balance sheet items, and the Directions allow the Reserve Bank to require more stringent standards for an individual bank. It applies on the same basis as the LCR. The courseware says the guidelines were issued on 17 May 2018 and came into effect on 1 October 2021 after a deferral for the pandemic; the Directions of 2025 give no effective date. ASF is the carrying value of capital and liabilities multiplied by the ASF factor of its category: 100 per cent for regulatory capital (excluding Tier 2 instruments with residual maturity under one year) and other capital instruments and liabilities with effective residual maturity of one year or more; 95 per cent for stable retail and small business deposits with residual maturity under one year; 90 per cent for less stable retail and small business deposits under one year; 50 per cent for funding under one year from non-financial corporates, operational deposits, funding under one year from sovereigns, public sector entities, multilateral and national development banks, and other funding of six months to under one year including from central banks and financial institutions; and zero per cent for all other liabilities (including funding from the central bank of under six months and liabilities with no stated maturity, subject to exceptions).
facts.locator: Printed p. 504-505, section 18.4 and Table 18.1; Directions paragraphs 205 to 225

facts.statement: Required stable funding is the carrying value of assets multiplied by the RSF factor: 0 per cent for coins and banknotes, CRR balances including excess, claims on the Reserve Bank with residual maturity under six months and trade-date receivables; 5 per cent for unencumbered Level 1 assets (other than those at zero) and unencumbered SLR securities; 10 per cent for unencumbered loans to financial institutions under six months secured by Level 1 assets that can be re-hypothecated; 15 per cent for unencumbered Level 2A assets and other standard unencumbered loans to financial institutions under six months; 50 per cent for unencumbered Level 2B assets, HQLA encumbered for six months to under one year, loans to financial institutions and central banks of six months to under one year, operational deposits at other financial institutions and other non-HQLA assets with residual maturity under one year including loans to non-financial corporates, retail and small business customers and sovereigns; 65 per cent for other unencumbered loans of one year or more (excluding loans to financial institutions) that qualify for a risk weight of 35 per cent or less; 85 per cent for initial margin and default fund contributions to a central counterparty, other performing loans of one year or more with a risk weight above 35 per cent, non-defaulted securities with remaining maturity of one year or more and exchange-traded equities, and physical traded commodities including gold; and 100 per cent for assets encumbered for one year or more, net derivative assets, 5 per cent of derivative liabilities and all other assets (including non-performing loans, fixed assets and non-exchange-traded equities). Off-balance sheet: 5 per cent of the currently undrawn portion of irrevocable and conditionally revocable credit and liquidity facilities and of other contingent funding obligations, and 3 per cent of the undrawn portion of trade finance related obligations including guarantees and letters of credit.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 505-508, Tables 18.2 and 18.3; Directions paragraphs 226 to 238

payload.title: Why Basel III added liquidity standards
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Lessons from the crisis**: **risk weights left to bank models** and **heavy reliance on wholesale funding**.

| Basel III measure | Aim |
| --- | --- |
| **Higher, better capital and buffers** | **absorb losses** |
| **Limits on internal models, risk weight floors** | **cut variation in risk weighted assets** |
| **Leverage ratio** | **non-risk-based backstop** |
| **LCR and NSFR** | **liquidity: short-term and longer-term** |

(The courseware says India's minimum capital adequacy ratio went **from 9% to 11.5%**, with **11.5%** a first trigger and **9%** a second leading to **Prompt Corrective Action**.)

| Standard | Horizon | Idea |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **LCR** | **30 days** | **enough high quality liquid assets to survive an acute stress** |
| **NSFR** | **one year** | **fund activities with more stable sources** |

The framework was issued **December 2010**; **five monitoring tools** supplement the two standards.

payload.title: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio
payload.core_explanation_md:
**LCR = Stock of HQLA ÷ Total net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar days**, **at least 100% on an ongoing basis**.

- The stock is a **defence against the onset of stress**: **in stress a bank may use it and fall below 100%**, but must **immediately report to the Department of Supervision, with reasons and corrective steps**.
- Aim: **survive to day 30**, when **corrective action is assumed**.
- **Scope** (Directions): **Indian banks on solo and consolidated basis**; **foreign bank branches in India on solo basis**.
- **History (courseware)**: **60% in 2015, rising 10 points a year to 100% in 2019**; **pandemic relaxation 80% then 90% until 31 March 2021**; **100% from 1 April 2021**.

**Stress scenario** (bank-specific plus market-wide): **retail deposit run-off; loss of unsecured wholesale funding; loss of secured short-term funding; downgrade of up to three notches with collateral calls; higher haircuts from volatility; draws on committed facilities; buy-back of debt or reputational obligations**.

payload.title: High quality liquid assets and the 15% and 40% caps
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Class | Examples | Haircut | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Level 1** | **cash and excess CRR; Standing Deposit Facility balances; Government securities above minimum SLR; qualifying zero-risk foreign sovereign securities** | **none** (but **from 1 April 2026** Government securities take **LAF/MSF haircuts**) | **no limit** |
| **Level 2A** | **qualifying less liquid assets** | **at least 15%** | **Level 2 total at most 40% of the stock** |
| **Level 2B** | **lower rated or riskier assets** | **at least 50%** | **at most 15% of the stock; inside the 40%** |

**Within the mandatory SLR**, Government securities count only up to **MSF (currently 2% of NDTL)** and **FALLCR (currently 16% of NDTL in the Directions; the courseware says 9%)**.

**FALLCR**: **stress only**, after **all other HQLA are used**, **declaration needed**, **up to 90 days**, **MSF haircuts**, **200 basis points over the LAF repo rate**.

**Stock = L1 + L2A + L2B − 15% cap adjustment − 40% cap adjustment**.

payload.title: Net cash outflows and the 75% inflow cap
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Net cash outflows (30 days) = Outflows − Min(Inflows, 75% × Outflows)**.

- **Outflows** = **balances × run-off rates**; **inflows** = **contractual receivables × inflow rates**, **capped at 75% of outflows**.
- **No double counting**: an asset counted in **HQLA** **cannot also be an inflow**.

| Retail deposit (natural persons) | Run-off |
| --- | --- |
| **Stable** (**DICGC-insured**, **transactional or relationship account**) | **5%** |
| **Less stable** | **10%** |
| **Stable with internet or mobile banking, from 1 April 2026** | **7.5%** |
| **Less stable with internet or mobile banking, from 1 April 2026** | **12.5%** |

**Small business customers** count as retail only if **aggregated funding is up to ₹7.5 crore**. **Unsecured wholesale funding** = **from non-natural persons, not secured on specific assets, callable or maturing within 30 days**.

payload.title: Monitoring tools, returns and disclosure
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Tool | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Contractual maturity mismatch** | **gaps between contractual inflows and outflows by time band**; reliance on **maturity transformation** |
| **Concentration of funding** | **significant counterparties, products and currencies**; **diversification** |
| **Available unencumbered assets** | **assets that could be pledged for funds** |
| **LCR by significant currency** | **currency mismatches** |
| **Market-related tools** | **high frequency market data as early warning** |

| Return | Content | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **BLR-1** | **LCR** | **monthly** |
| **BLR-2** | **funding concentration** | **monthly** |
| **BLR-3** | **available unencumbered assets** | **quarterly** |
| **BLR-4** | **LCR by significant currency** | **monthly** |
| **BLR-5** | **other liquidity information** | **monthly** |

In stress the **Reserve Bank may direct weekly or even daily LCR reporting**; the bank must be **able to do so**.

payload.title: The Net Stable Funding Ratio and available stable funding
payload.core_explanation_md:
**NSFR = Available stable funding ÷ Required stable funding**, **at least 100% on an ongoing basis**, **one-year horizon**, **reported quarterly**; the Reserve Bank may **require stricter standards** for an individual bank.

| ASF factor | Liabilities |
| --- | --- |
| **100%** | **regulatory capital** (not Tier 2 under a year) and **liabilities of one year or more** |
| **95%** | **stable retail and small business deposits under one year** |
| **90%** | **less stable retail and small business deposits under one year** |
| **50%** | **non-financial corporate funding under one year; operational deposits; sovereign, public sector and development bank funding under one year; other funding of 6 months to under 1 year** |
| **0%** | **everything else**, including **central bank funding under 6 months** |

(The courseware says the guidelines were issued **17 May 2018** and applied from **1 October 2021**.)

payload.title: Required stable funding factors
payload.core_explanation_md:
| RSF factor | Assets |
| --- | --- |
| **0%** | **coins and notes; CRR balances; claims on the Reserve Bank under 6 months** |
| **5%** | **unencumbered Level 1 (other than at 0%) and unencumbered SLR securities** |
| **10%** | **loans to financial institutions under 6 months secured by Level 1 assets** |
| **15%** | **unencumbered Level 2A; other loans to financial institutions under 6 months** |
| **50%** | **Level 2B; HQLA encumbered 6 to 12 months; other assets maturing under a year, including loans to corporates, retail and sovereigns** |
| **65%** | **loans of one year or more with risk weight of 35% or less** |
| **85%** | **initial margin and CCP default fund; other performing loans of one year or more (risk weight above 35%); securities of one year or more; listed equities; gold** |
| **100%** | **assets encumbered one year or more; non-performing loans; fixed assets; all others** |

**Off-balance sheet**: **5% of the undrawn portion** of **credit and liquidity facilities and other contingent funding**; **3% of the undrawn portion** of **trade finance obligations, guarantees and letters of credit**.

payload.title: Applying the 15% and 40% caps
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: after haircuts a bank holds Level 1 assets of ₹400 crore, Level 2A of ₹300 crore and Level 2B of ₹200 crore. Compute the stock of HQLA under the Directions' formula.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: The stock of HQLA is ₹666.67 crore, with Level 1 at 60% and Level 2 at 40%

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the stock of HQLA smaller than the sum of the three levels?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Level 2B above 15% and Level 2 above 40% of the stock cannot count, so the caps remove the excess.

payload.title: Retail deposit run-off after April 2026
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank has stable retail deposits of ₹4,000 crore without internet or mobile banking and ₹2,000 crore with it, and less stable retail deposits of ₹3,000 crore without and ₹1,000 crore with it. Find the retail deposit outflow for the LCR from 1 April 2026.

worked_steps.description: Stable, no internet or mobile banking, at 5%.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The retail deposit outflow is ₹775 crore

self_check.prompt_text: What does the extra 2.5 percentage points reflect?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Deposits that can be withdrawn through internet and mobile banking can run off faster in stress, so they carry a higher run-off rate.

payload.title: The LCR with the inflow cap
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank has weighted total expected outflows of ₹900 crore, weighted total expected inflows of ₹800 crore and a stock of HQLA of ₹270 crore. Find the net cash outflows and the LCR.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: Net cash outflows are ₹225 crore and the LCR is 120%, above the 100% minimum

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the inflow figure limited to ₹675 crore rather than ₹800 crore?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Inflows are capped at 75 per cent of outflows so that a bank cannot rely wholly on inflows and must keep a stock of HQLA.

payload.title: A simple NSFR
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank has capital and liabilities of one year or more of ₹1,000 crore, stable retail deposits under one year of ₹2,000 crore, less stable retail deposits of ₹1,000 crore and non-financial corporate funding under one year of ₹1,500 crore. Its assets are CRR balances ₹300 crore, unencumbered SLR securities ₹1,000 crore, unencumbered Level 2A assets ₹200 crore, loans to non-financial corporates under one year ₹1,500 crore, loans of one year or more with a risk weight of 35% or less ₹2,000 crore, other performing loans of one year or more with a higher risk weight ₹1,500 crore, and undrawn irrevocable credit lines of ₹400 crore. Compute the NSFR.

worked_steps.description: ASF from capital and long liabilities at 100%.
ASF from less stable retail at 90%.
RSF on CRR (0%), SLR securities (5%), Level 2A (15%).

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The NSFR is 132.85%, above the 100% minimum

self_check.prompt_text: Which asset line contributes most to required stable funding, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The long loans of one year or more, because they carry the high 65 and 85 per cent factors for being illiquid and long-dated.

payload.stem_md: Which Basel III measure is a simple, non-risk-based backstop to the risk-based capital requirements?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The leverage ratio is a simple, transparent, non-risk-based measure that backs up the risk-based requirements.

payload.stem_md: Over what time horizon does the Net Stable Funding Ratio promote resilience?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The NSFR extends to one year, while the LCR covers 30 days.

payload.stem_md: Why do the LCR and NSFR complement each other?

options.text_md: The NSFR replaces the LCR after a year
The LCR covers short-term resilience through liquid assets, and the NSFR covers longer-term resilience through stable funding

payload.correct_explanation_md: They achieve two separate but complementary objectives: 30-day survival and a stable funding profile over one year.

payload.stem_md: What is the minimum Liquidity Coverage Ratio that a bank must maintain on an ongoing basis under the Directions?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The LCR must be at a minimum of 100 per cent on an ongoing basis; the phase-in is complete.

payload.stem_md: A bank uses its stock of HQLA in a financial stress and its LCR falls below 100 per cent. What must it do?

options.text_md: Nothing, since the minimum applies only in normal times
Immediately report the shortfall, reasons and corrective steps to the Department of Supervision

payload.correct_explanation_md: A bank may use its HQLA in stress but shall immediately report the shortfall with reasons and corrective steps.

payload.stem_md: The LCR stress scenario assumes a downgrade in the bank's public credit rating by up to how many notches?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The scenario includes additional contractual outflows from a downgrade of up to three notches.

payload.stem_md: To what level do the Directions apply the LCR framework for an Indian bank?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The LCR framework applies to an Indian bank on a standalone as well as consolidated level.

payload.stem_md: Which asset is a Level 1 high quality liquid asset?

options.text_md: Government securities in excess of the minimum SLR requirement

payload.correct_explanation_md: Government securities in excess of the minimum SLR are Level 1 assets.

payload.stem_md: What is the minimum haircut on a Level 2B asset in the stock of HQLA?
payload.correct_explanation_md: A minimum haircut of 50 per cent applies to each Level 2B asset.

payload.stem_md: What is the maximum share of Level 2 assets (after haircuts) in the overall stock of HQLA?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Level 2 assets, after haircuts, shall be no more than 40 per cent of the stock.

payload.stem_md: Under FALLCR, at what rate is funds availed against Government securities within the mandatory SLR?

options.text_md: The same as the repo rate
2 per cent below the repo rate
200 basis points above the LAF repo rate

payload.correct_explanation_md: The facility rate is 200 bps above the prevailing LAF repo rate for up to 90 days.

payload.stem_md: Under the Directions, what share of NDTL is currently allowed under FALLCR (within the mandatory SLR) for LCR purposes?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The Directions say FALLCR is currently 16 per cent of NDTL, with MSF at 2 per cent.

payload.stem_md: How are total net cash outflows computed?

options.text_md: Total expected outflows less the smaller of total expected inflows and 75 per cent of outflows

payload.correct_explanation_md: Net outflows equal outflows minus min(inflows, 75 per cent of outflows).

payload.stem_md: Which retail deposits are classified as stable for the LCR?

options.text_md: Deposits insured by the DICGC, in transactional or relationship accounts

payload.correct_explanation_md: Stable deposits are insured deposits, to the extent covered by DICGC, in transactional or relationship-based accounts.

payload.stem_md: From 1 April 2026, what run-off rate applies to stable retail deposits enabled with internet and mobile banking?
payload.correct_explanation_md: An additional 2.5 per cent applies, so stable deposits with internet and mobile banking carry 7.5 per cent.

payload.stem_md: Up to what aggregated funding is a small business customer's deposit treated like retail for the LCR?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Funding from a small business customer is treated as retail if the total aggregated funding is up to ₹7.5 crore.

payload.stem_md: A bank holds a Government security in its stock of HQLA. How should the cash inflows from that security be treated?

options.text_md: Counted as an inflow as well
They must not be counted again as inflows in the denominator

payload.correct_explanation_md: If an asset is included in the HQLA stock, its associated cash inflows shall not be counted as inflows.

payload.stem_md: Which return reports the LCR by significant currency?
payload.correct_explanation_md: BLR-4 is the statement on LCR by significant currency, submitted monthly.

payload.stem_md: Which liquidity return is submitted quarterly rather than monthly?
payload.correct_explanation_md: BLR-3 is quarterly; the others are monthly.

payload.stem_md: What does the concentration of funding metric monitor?

options.text_md: Funding from each significant counterparty, instrument and currency

payload.correct_explanation_md: The metric monitors funding from each significant counterparty, significant product or instrument and significant currency.

payload.stem_md: What ASF factor applies to stable retail deposits with residual maturity under one year?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Stable retail and small business deposits under one year receive a 95 per cent ASF factor.

payload.stem_md: What ASF factor applies to funding with residual maturity under one year from non-financial corporate customers?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Funding under one year from non-financial corporate customers receives 50 per cent.

payload.stem_md: What is the minimum Net Stable Funding Ratio?
payload.correct_explanation_md: A bank shall maintain an NSFR of at least 100 per cent on an ongoing basis.

payload.stem_md: What RSF factor applies to unencumbered SLR securities?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Unencumbered Level 1 assets and unencumbered SLR securities receive a 5 per cent RSF factor.

payload.stem_md: What RSF factor applies to the undrawn portion of trade finance obligations such as guarantees and letters of credit?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The undrawn portion of trade finance related obligations carries 3 per cent; credit and liquidity facilities carry 5 per cent.

payload.stem_md: The stock of HQLA of a bank, after haircuts and caps, is ₹8,000 crore. What is the most that Level 2B assets can be, in ₹ crore?
A bank holds Level 2A securities with a market value of ₹500 crore. What value do they contribute to the stock of HQLA at the minimum haircut, in ₹ crore?
A bank holds Level 2B assets with a market value of ₹300 crore. What value do they contribute at the minimum haircut, in ₹ crore?
Weighted total expected outflows are ₹1,600 crore and weighted total expected inflows are ₹1,500 crore. What are the total net cash outflows, in ₹ crore?
A bank has a stock of HQLA of ₹540 crore and total net cash outflows of ₹400 crore. What is its LCR, in per cent, to two decimals?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.stem_md: A bank has stable retail deposits under one year of ₹3,000 crore, less stable retail deposits of ₹1,000 crore and non-financial corporate funding under one year of ₹800 crore. What is the available stable funding from these, in ₹ crore?

A bank has NDTL of ₹50,000 crore. What is the most Government securities within the mandatory SLR that can count as Level 1 HQLA under MSF and FALLCR together, at the current 2 per cent and 16 per cent of NDTL, in ₹ crore?
A bank has ₹600 crore of undrawn irrevocable credit facilities and ₹500 crore of undrawn trade finance guarantees. What is the total RSF for these off-balance sheet items, in ₹ crore?

unresolved: The Directions copy read is the mirror of the 28 November 2025 text; later circulars on run-off rates, FALLCR and the haircut changes announced for 1 April 2026 were not searched for beyond that text. The 1 April 2026 changes (Government security haircuts, additional run-off for internet and mobile banking deposits, deposits pledged against loans) are taught as stated in the Directions.

The courseware describes FALLCR at 9 per cent of NDTL and solo-level LCR scope; the Directions say 16 per cent and standalone plus consolidated. The Directions are used. The courseware's phase-in and pandemic relaxation are historical and are taught as the courseware's account.

Run-off rates for other categories of unsecured wholesale funding, secured funding, derivatives, committed facilities and inflow rates were not taught or tested beyond retail deposits and the 75 per cent inflow cap; the liquidity return (BLR-1) lists them.

The courseware's statements that the NSFR guidelines were issued on 17 May 2018 and came into effect on 1 October 2021 are the courseware's account; the Directions of 2025 give no effective date. The courseware's time limits for submitting returns are not in the Directions and are not tested.

The courseware's statement that the minimum capital adequacy ratio moved from 9 per cent to 11.5 per cent is taught as the courseware's account (9 per cent minimum plus a 2.5 per cent conservation buffer); it was not rechecked in this batch.
Intraday liquidity (Chapter IV) and interest rate risk (Chapter VII) of the Directions are not covered here.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.

items.title: Why Basel III added liquidity standards
items.core_explanation_md:
**Lessons from the crisis**: **risk weights left to bank models** and **heavy reliance on wholesale funding**.

| Basel III measure | Aim |
| --- | --- |
| **Higher, better capital and buffers** | **absorb losses** |
| **Limits on internal models, risk weight floors** | **cut variation in risk weighted assets** |
| **Leverage ratio** | **non-risk-based backstop** |
| **LCR and NSFR** | **liquidity: short-term and longer-term** |

(The courseware says India's minimum capital adequacy ratio went **from 9% to 11.5%**, with **11.5%** a first trigger and **9%** a second leading to **Prompt Corrective Action**.)

| Standard | Horizon | Idea |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **LCR** | **30 days** | **enough high quality liquid assets to survive an acute stress** |
| **NSFR** | **one year** | **fund activities with more stable sources** |

The framework was issued **December 2010**; **five monitoring tools** supplement the two standards.

items.title: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio
items.core_explanation_md:
**LCR = Stock of HQLA ÷ Total net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar days**, **at least 100% on an ongoing basis**.

- The stock is a **defence against the onset of stress**: **in stress a bank may use it and fall below 100%**, but must **immediately report to the Department of Supervision, with reasons and corrective steps**.
- Aim: **survive to day 30**, when **corrective action is assumed**.
- **Scope** (Directions): **Indian banks on solo and consolidated basis**; **foreign bank branches in India on solo basis**.
- **History (courseware)**: **60% in 2015, rising 10 points a year to 100% in 2019**; **pandemic relaxation 80% then 90% until 31 March 2021**; **100% from 1 April 2021**.

**Stress scenario** (bank-specific plus market-wide): **retail deposit run-off; loss of unsecured wholesale funding; loss of secured short-term funding; downgrade of up to three notches with collateral calls; higher haircuts from volatility; draws on committed facilities; buy-back of debt or reputational obligations**.

items.title: High quality liquid assets and the 15% and 40% caps
items.core_explanation_md:
| Class | Examples | Haircut | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Level 1** | **cash and excess CRR; Standing Deposit Facility balances; Government securities above minimum SLR; qualifying zero-risk foreign sovereign securities** | **none** (but **from 1 April 2026** Government securities take **LAF/MSF haircuts**) | **no limit** |
| **Level 2A** | **qualifying less liquid assets** | **at least 15%** | **Level 2 total at most 40% of the stock** |
| **Level 2B** | **lower rated or riskier assets** | **at least 50%** | **at most 15% of the stock; inside the 40%** |

**Within the mandatory SLR**, Government securities count only up to **MSF (currently 2% of NDTL)** and **FALLCR (currently 16% of NDTL in the Directions; the courseware says 9%)**.

**FALLCR**: **stress only**, after **all other HQLA are used**, **declaration needed**, **up to 90 days**, **MSF haircuts**, **200 basis points over the LAF repo rate**.

**Stock = L1 + L2A + L2B − 15% cap adjustment − 40% cap adjustment**.

items.title: Net cash outflows and the 75% inflow cap
items.core_explanation_md:
**Net cash outflows (30 days) = Outflows − Min(Inflows, 75% × Outflows)**.

- **Outflows** = **balances × run-off rates**; **inflows** = **contractual receivables × inflow rates**, **capped at 75% of outflows**.
- **No double counting**: an asset counted in **HQLA** **cannot also be an inflow**.

| Retail deposit (natural persons) | Run-off |
| --- | --- |
| **Stable** (**DICGC-insured**, **transactional or relationship account**) | **5%** |
| **Less stable** | **10%** |
| **Stable with internet or mobile banking, from 1 April 2026** | **7.5%** |
| **Less stable with internet or mobile banking, from 1 April 2026** | **12.5%** |

**Small business customers** count as retail only if **aggregated funding is up to ₹7.5 crore**. **Unsecured wholesale funding** = **from non-natural persons, not secured on specific assets, callable or maturing within 30 days**.

items.title: Monitoring tools, returns and disclosure
items.core_explanation_md:
| Tool | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Contractual maturity mismatch** | **gaps between contractual inflows and outflows by time band**; reliance on **maturity transformation** |
| **Concentration of funding** | **significant counterparties, products and currencies**; **diversification** |
| **Available unencumbered assets** | **assets that could be pledged for funds** |
| **LCR by significant currency** | **currency mismatches** |
| **Market-related tools** | **high frequency market data as early warning** |

| Return | Content | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **BLR-1** | **LCR** | **monthly** |
| **BLR-2** | **funding concentration** | **monthly** |
| **BLR-3** | **available unencumbered assets** | **quarterly** |
| **BLR-4** | **LCR by significant currency** | **monthly** |
| **BLR-5** | **other liquidity information** | **monthly** |

In stress the **Reserve Bank may direct weekly or even daily LCR reporting**; the bank must be **able to do so**.

items.title: The Net Stable Funding Ratio and available stable funding
items.core_explanation_md:
**NSFR = Available stable funding ÷ Required stable funding**, **at least 100% on an ongoing basis**, **one-year horizon**, **reported quarterly**; the Reserve Bank may **require stricter standards** for an individual bank.

| ASF factor | Liabilities |
| --- | --- |
| **100%** | **regulatory capital** (not Tier 2 under a year) and **liabilities of one year or more** |
| **95%** | **stable retail and small business deposits under one year** |
| **90%** | **less stable retail and small business deposits under one year** |
| **50%** | **non-financial corporate funding under one year; operational deposits; sovereign, public sector and development bank funding under one year; other funding of 6 months to under 1 year** |
| **0%** | **everything else**, including **central bank funding under 6 months** |

(The courseware says the guidelines were issued **17 May 2018** and applied from **1 October 2021**.)

items.title: Required stable funding factors
items.core_explanation_md:
| RSF factor | Assets |
| --- | --- |
| **0%** | **coins and notes; CRR balances; claims on the Reserve Bank under 6 months** |
| **5%** | **unencumbered Level 1 (other than at 0%) and unencumbered SLR securities** |
| **10%** | **loans to financial institutions under 6 months secured by Level 1 assets** |
| **15%** | **unencumbered Level 2A; other loans to financial institutions under 6 months** |
| **50%** | **Level 2B; HQLA encumbered 6 to 12 months; other assets maturing under a year, including loans to corporates, retail and sovereigns** |
| **65%** | **loans of one year or more with risk weight of 35% or less** |
| **85%** | **initial margin and CCP default fund; other performing loans of one year or more (risk weight above 35%); securities of one year or more; listed equities; gold** |
| **100%** | **assets encumbered one year or more; non-performing loans; fixed assets; all others** |

**Off-balance sheet**: **5% of the undrawn portion** of **credit and liquidity facilities and other contingent funding**; **3% of the undrawn portion** of **trade finance obligations, guarantees and letters of credit**.

items.title: Applying the 15% and 40% caps
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: after haircuts a bank holds Level 1 assets of ₹400 crore, Level 2A of ₹300 crore and Level 2B of ₹200 crore. Compute the stock of HQLA under the Directions' formula.
items.final_answer_with_unit: The stock of HQLA is ₹666.67 crore, with Level 1 at 60% and Level 2 at 40%

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the stock of HQLA smaller than the sum of the three levels?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Level 2B above 15% and Level 2 above 40% of the stock cannot count, so the caps remove the excess.

items.title: Retail deposit run-off after April 2026
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank has stable retail deposits of ₹4,000 crore without internet or mobile banking and ₹2,000 crore with it, and less stable retail deposits of ₹3,000 crore without and ₹1,000 crore with it. Find the retail deposit outflow for the LCR from 1 April 2026.

worked_steps.description: Stable, no internet or mobile banking, at 5%.

items.final_answer_with_unit: The retail deposit outflow is ₹775 crore

self_check.prompt_text: What does the extra 2.5 percentage points reflect?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Deposits that can be withdrawn through internet and mobile banking can run off faster in stress, so they carry a higher run-off rate.

items.title: A simple NSFR
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank has capital and liabilities of one year or more of ₹1,000 crore, stable retail deposits under one year of ₹2,000 crore, less stable retail deposits of ₹1,000 crore and non-financial corporate funding under one year of ₹1,500 crore. Its assets are CRR balances ₹300 crore, unencumbered SLR securities ₹1,000 crore, unencumbered Level 2A assets ₹200 crore, loans to non-financial corporates under one year ₹1,500 crore, loans of one year or more with a risk weight of 35% or less ₹2,000 crore, other performing loans of one year or more with a higher risk weight ₹1,500 crore, and undrawn irrevocable credit lines of ₹400 crore. Compute the NSFR.

worked_steps.description: ASF from capital and long liabilities at 100%.
ASF from less stable retail at 90%.
RSF on CRR (0%), SLR securities (5%), Level 2A (15%).

items.final_answer_with_unit: The NSFR is 132.85%, above the 100% minimum

self_check.prompt_text: Which asset line contributes most to required stable funding, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The long loans of one year or more, because they carry the high 65 and 85 per cent factors for being illiquid and long-dated.
